title: Molecular characterization of a rare norovirus GII.8[P8] strain detected during pediatric acute gastroenteritis surveillance in Harbin, China

analysis.research_question_and_background: Norovirus is a leading cause of pediatric acute gastroenteritis, yet the rare GII.8[P8] genotype remains under-characterized due to limited whole-genome data.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A GII.8[P8] norovirus strain, Harbin-Nov-076-2022, was identified through routine pediatric acute gastroenteritis surveillance in Harbin, China.
analysis.methods: The strain was recovered from a stool sample of a 15-month-old female patient and sequenced on the DNBSEQ-T7 platform, followed by phylogenetic reconstruction, amino acid entropy profiling, selection pressure assessment, homology modeling of the capsid P protein, and B-cell epitope prediction.
analysis.main_results: The near-complete genome of Harbin-Nov-076-2022 is 7486 nt long with 53.81% GC content, assigned to the GII.8[P8] lineage and showing 97.52% nucleotide identity to the Thai 2018 strain GII/Hu/TH/2018/GII.8[P8]/B6213.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study expands whole-genome evidence for GII.8[P8] in Northeast China and identifies localized sequence-associated variations in the P2 subdomain and HBGA-binding loops, alongside 59 predicted B-cell epitopes.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings provide regional genomic data to inform molecular surveillance, evolutionary assessment, and antigenic characterization of non-dominant norovirus genotypes.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited by the single-strain analysis and absence of functional validation of predicted epitopes, warranting a moderate confidence assessment.

analysis.summary_en: This study characterized a rare norovirus GII.8[P8] strain, Harbin-Nov-076-2022, detected during pediatric acute gastroenteritis surveillance in Harbin, China. Whole-genome sequencing revealed a 7486 nt genome with 53.81% GC content and 97.52% nucleotide identity to a Thai 2018 reference. Phylogenetic assignment confirmed the GII.8[P8] lineage, while amino acid variability was highest in VP2 with three variable sites. Selection pressure analysis indicated purifying selection across the genome. Homology modeling predicted localized sequence-associated variations in the P2 subdomain and HBGA-binding loops, and 59 B-cell epitopes were predicted. The findings expand whole-genome evidence for this rare genotype and provide regional genomic data to support molecular surveillance, evolutionary assessment, and antigenic characterization of non-dominant norovirus genotypes.

title: Viral gastroenteritis: Molecular epidemiology of human norovirus by RT-PCR at University Hospital Center of Brazzaville, Republic of Congo

analysis.research_question_and_background: Acute gastroenteritis (AGE) is a major public health concern in Africa, with noroviruses recognized as predominant viral etiological agents. However, their epidemiological impact remains underreported in the Republic of Congo, particularly in Brazzaville.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted from June to November 2020 at the University Hospital Center of Brazzaville. Fifty children aged 28 days to 17 years presenting with AGE were enrolled, with eighty percent aged ≤5 years.
analysis.methods: Stool samples were analyzed using real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) to detect viral RNA and differentiate between GI and GII genogroups.
analysis.main_results: The overall prevalence of norovirus infection was 44%, with GII (73%) predominating over GI (18%). GI/GII co-infections were detected in 9% of cases. A significant association was observed between age and norovirus genogroup distribution (p = 0.03), with GII being more prevalent among children aged ≤5 years.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Norovirus represents an important cause of pediatric AGE in Brazzaville. The study identified circulating genogroups and highlighted age-related distribution differences, contributing to local molecular epidemiology knowledge.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings support the integration of molecular diagnostic approaches into national surveillance programs and the strengthening of sanitation measures to improve prevention and control strategies for norovirus gastroenteritis.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study’s cross-sectional design and small sample size limit causal inference and generalizability. The evidence strength is assessed as moderate due to potential selection bias and lack of longitudinal follow-up.

analysis.summary_en: This study assessed the molecular epidemiology of human norovirus among children with acute gastroenteritis in Brazzaville, Republic of Congo. Using RT-PCR, it detected norovirus in 44% of 50 enrolled children, with GII genogroups predominating (73%) and a significant age-related distribution (p = 0.03). Co-infections were present in 9% of cases. The authors conclude norovirus is a major pediatric AGE pathogen locally and recommend integrating molecular diagnostics into surveillance and improving sanitation. Limitations include a small sample size, cross-sectional design, and potential selection bias, warranting cautious interpretation.

title: Zymosan-adjuvanted intranasal norovirus virus-like particle vaccine induces antiviral mucosal immune responses in infant mice.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the need for pain-free mucosal vaccines optimized for infants, as their immune systems are weaker than adults, necessitating repeated immunizations with injectable vaccines that cause discomfort.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used an infant murine model to examine the effectiveness of an intranasal norovirus virus-like-particle (VLP) vaccine with zymosan as an adjuvant.
analysis.methods: The researchers administered the vaccine to infant mice and measured immune responses, including levels of VLP-specific IgA antibodies in intestinal and salivary tissues, as well as VLP-specific IgG antibodies in plasma.
analysis.main_results: Infant mice given a minimum dose of the zymosan-adjuvanted VLP vaccine showed increased levels of intestinal and salivary VLP-specific IgA antibodies, as well as plasma VLP-specific IgG antibodies, comparable to those in adults.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that the zymosan-adjuvanted norovirus VLP vaccine can induce effective mucosal immune responses in infants, potentially reducing the need for painful injections.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results may inform the development of mucosal vaccines for infants, offering a non-invasive alternative to injectable vaccines and improving compliance with immunization schedules.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to an infant murine model, which may not fully represent human immune responses, but the evidence is strong due to direct comparisons with adult responses and biological relevance.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the potential of a zymosan-adjuvanted intranasal norovirus virus-like particle (VLP) vaccine to induce mucosal immune responses in infant mice. The research was motivated by the need for pain-free and effective vaccines for infants, as their immune systems are less mature and injectable vaccines are uncomfortable. The study used an infant murine model to evaluate the vaccine's effectiveness, finding that it induced immune responses comparable to those in adults. These results suggest that the vaccine could be a promising candidate for infant immunization against norovirus, potentially reducing the need for multiple painful injections. The findings have implications for developing non-invasive vaccines for infants, which could improve immunization compliance and effectiveness. However, the study's reliance on a murine model limits the direct applicability of the results to humans, though the evidence is strong and relevant.

title: Norovirus on Cruise Ships: A Recurring Sentinel Event

analysis.scope_and_question: Norovirus remains the leading cause of acute gastroenteritis outbreaks worldwide and is particularly well adapted for transmission aboard cruise ships due to its low infectious dose, prolonged environmental persistence, and rapid person-to-person spread.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: We reviewed recent outbreaks to highlight recurring norovirus outbreaks and gaps in maritime surveillance.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: These demonstrate the vulnerability of cruise ships to rapid viral amplification and international dissemination.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Current surveillance relies predominantly on symptomatic case reporting, limiting the ability to distinguish between single-source introduction, environmental persistence, foodborne transmission, and emergence of novel recombinant strains.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Recent modelling studies have shown that early diagnosis and isolation of symptomatic individuals substantially reduce secondary transmission, yet routine genomic surveillance is rarely implemented onboard.

analysis.summary_en: This review focuses on norovirus as the primary pathogen causing acute gastroenteritis outbreaks on cruise ships. The study highlights the virus's adaptability to maritime environments due to its low infectious dose, environmental persistence, and rapid spread. The evidence base includes recent outbreaks and modeling studies, which emphasize the need for improved surveillance and infection control measures. Current methods rely heavily on symptomatic reporting, which limits the ability to differentiate transmission routes. The review underscores the importance of integrating wastewater-based and genomic surveillance to enhance outbreak detection and control. Despite the potential benefits of early diagnosis and isolation, genomic surveillance is not routinely implemented on cruise ships. The findings suggest that strengthening surveillance systems and infection control protocols could improve global preparedness for norovirus outbreaks associated with international travel.

title: Treatment With Ruxolitinib and TAK-779 Enhances GII.17 Human Norovirus Replication and Enables Serial Passaging in Human Intestinal Enteroids.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Human norovirus (HuNoV) is a major cause of acute viral gastroenteritis. Although it can be replicated in vitro using human intestinal enteroids (HIEs), generating high-titer viral laboratory stocks remains challenging due to low infection and passage efficiencies.

title: Clinical characteristics associated with gastrointestinal bleeding in neonates with laboratory-confirmed norovirus gastroenteritis

analysis.research_question_and_background: Norovirus (NoV) is a major cause of acute gastroenteritis in children, but pathogen-confirmed data in neonates remain limited, particularly regarding clinical differences associated with gastrointestinal bleeding.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We conducted a single-center retrospective observational study of neonates younger than 28 days who were hospitalized at the Children's Hospital of Soochow University between December 31, 2024 and December 31, 2025, had positive stool NoV antigen results, and underwent confirmatory nucleic acid testing.
analysis.methods: After excluding clinically identifiable alternative causes of gastrointestinal bleeding, patients were classified into hemorrhagic and non-hemorrhagic groups. Baseline characteristics, clinical manifestations, comorbidities, and laboratory findings obtained within 24 h after admission were compared between groups. Laboratory variables showing significant between-group differences were entered into a multivariable logistic regression model.
analysis.main_results: A total of 139 neonates were included, comprising 52 in the hemorrhagic group and 87 in the non-hemorrhagic group. Among the hemorrhagic cases, 49 had overt gastrointestinal bleeding and three had isolated fecal occult blood positivity.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The hemorrhagic group had a higher frequency of diarrhea and a lower frequency of jaundice. Hemoglobin, total bilirubin, indirect bilirubin, aspartate aminotransferase, the aspartate aminotransferase/alanine aminotransferase ratio, pH-corrected venous ionized calcium, chloride, and lactate were lower in the hemorrhagic group, whereas blood base excess was higher.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that specific clinical and laboratory features may be associated with gastrointestinal bleeding in neonates with norovirus gastroenteritis, which could inform targeted surveillance and management strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The association with lower ionized calcium should be interpreted cautiously because of the retrospective design and potential residual confounding.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated clinical characteristics associated with gastrointestinal bleeding in neonates with laboratory-confirmed norovirus gastroenteritis. A single-center retrospective observational study was conducted on 139 neonates hospitalized between December 31, 2024, and December 31, 2025, at the Children's Hospital of Soochow University. Neonates were classified into hemorrhagic and non-hemorrhagic groups after excluding alternative causes of bleeding. Baseline characteristics, clinical manifestations, comorbidities, and laboratory findings were compared between groups. The hemorrhagic group showed a higher frequency of diarrhea and lower levels of hemoglobin, total bilirubin, and ionized calcium, along with higher blood base excess. A multivariable logistic regression model found that each 0.1 mmol/L increase in ionized calcium was associated with lower odds of the hemorrhagic phenotype. The study highlights potential clinical and laboratory markers for gastrointestinal bleeding in neonates with norovirus infection, which could aid in targeted surveillance and management. However, the retrospective design and potential residual confounding limit the strength of the findings.

title: A contamination-free lateral flow platform for point-of-care virus detection in wastewater

analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved the development and validation of a closed reaction system for detecting norovirus and rotavirus in wastewater samples collected from a municipal treatment plant in China over 12 months. The platform was tested on 28 wastewater samples, with each sample analyzed for both target viruses.
analysis.methods: The platform utilized recombinase polymerase amplification combined with CRISPR-associated protein 13a lateral flow assay. Performance was evaluated through analytical sensitivity, specificity, and agreement with quantitative polymerase chain reaction.
analysis.main_results: The optimized assay achieved a limit of detection of 1 attomolar in approximately 90 minutes and showed no cross-reactivity with tested non-target viruses. analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The platform offers a portable solution for wastewater-based surveillance, which can enhance early warning systems for infectious disease outbreaks and support real-time public health monitoring.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's evidence is limited to synthetic RNA standards and 28 wastewater samples, which may affect generalizability. The platform combines recombinase polymerase amplification with CRISPR-associated protein 13a and gold nanoparticle-based detection. The results showed no cross-reactivity with non-target viruses and 14 positive detections across 56 tests, comparable to quantitative polymerase chain reaction. The findings highlight the platform's potential for enhancing wastewater-based epidemiology and public health surveillance. However, the study's limited sample size and reliance on synthetic standards may affect generalizability, resulting in moderate confidence in the results.

title: Emergence of a novel GII.17 variant is associated with immune evasion rather than an altered HBGA-binding profile

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate whether the surge in GII.17 norovirus detection in 2024 was due to changes in binding and antigenicity, which could explain its increased prevalence and immune evasion capabilities.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study compared the properties of a GII.17 2024 strain with representative GII.17 strains from 2005, 2014, and 2015, as well as the GII.4 Sydney 2012 variant. It focused on the antigenic and HBGA-binding profiles of these strains.
analysis.methods: Binding to saliva samples and human intestinal tissues with different HBGA profiles was assessed using norovirus virus-like particles (VLPs). analysis.main_results: The 2024 GII.17 strain showed amino acid substitutions in the P2 domain, which includes both antigenic sites and the HBGA binding site. All post-2005 GII.17 strains exhibited a broader HBGA binding profile compared to the 2005 strain.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that the recent re-emergence of GII.17 is linked to antigenic drift rather than changes in HBGA binding specificity, allowing it to evade pre-existing immunity.

The research compares the antigenic and HBGA-binding profiles of the 2024 strain with historical GII.17 strains and the GII.4 Sydney 2012 variant. Results show that the 2024 strain has amino acid substitutions in the P2 domain, which may contribute to immune evasion. Binding-blocking assays with sera from different time periods reveal that the 2024 variant is antigenically distinct from earlier GII.17 strains but closely related to the 2014 variant. The broader HBGA binding profile of post-2005 GII.17 strains is likely a factor in their increased spread. The study suggests that the recent re-emergence of GII.17 is due to antigenic drift rather than changes in HBGA binding, which has implications for vaccine development and surveillance. However, the study is limited by its use of sera from healthy adults and the absence of direct clinical outcomes, resulting in moderate evidence strength.

title: Breastfeeding and viral infections in preterm infants: a multicenter cohort study.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to evaluate the effect of breastfeeding status up to 6 months of age on the incidence of viral infections during the first year of life in preterm infants.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Data were obtained from the Japanese National Hospital Organization Neonatal Intensive Care Unit Registry for the periods 2010-2014 and 2016-2018. Information on breastfeeding exposure and infection history was collected through parental questionnaires administered when the infants reached one year of age. A total of 3,368 preterm infants who completed follow-up at one year were analyzed.
analysis.methods: The risk ratio (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were estimated using a modified Poisson regression model to evaluate the association between breastfeeding and the risk of viral infections, including influenza virus, respiratory syncytial (RS) virus, rotavirus, and norovirus.
analysis.main_results: Breastfeeding was associated with a lower risk of influenza infection (adjusted RR: 0.66, 95% CI: 0.48-0.89) and indicated a trend toward lower risk for other viral infections.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Breastfeeding for up to 6 months may lower the risk of viral infections in preterm infants, suggesting that providing breastfeeding support could contribute to improved health outcomes.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings support the promotion of breastfeeding in preterm infants as part of infection prevention strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Given the vulnerability of preterm infants, further research is required to confirm these associations and to evaluate the long-term health implications of breastfeeding.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the impact of breastfeeding on viral infections in preterm infants, focusing on norovirus and other related viruses. It used a multicenter cohort design, collecting data from the Japanese National Hospital Organization Neonatal Intensive Care Unit Registry between 2010-2014 and 2016-2018. Parental questionnaires were used to gather information on breastfeeding exposure and infection history, with 3,368 preterm infants included in the analysis. The study found that breastfeeding was associated with a lower risk of influenza infection and showed a trend toward lower risk for other viral infections, including norovirus. The authors suggest that breastfeeding support may improve health outcomes in preterm infants. However, they note the need for further research to confirm these associations and assess long-term implications. The evidence is moderate, as the study relies on self-reported data and does not account for all potential confounding factors.

title: Living with Primary Immunodeficiencies: CVID—Enteropathy from the Perspective of a Gastroenterologist

analysis.scope_and_question: Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID), the most prevalent symptomatic primary antibody deficiency (∼1:25,000), in its symptomatic spectrum reaches way beyond intractable, chronic, and recurrent infections. Noninfectious enteropathy (CVID-E)—affecting 15–30% of patients—has emerged as a pivotal manifestation of the natural disease trajectory, with approximately 11-fold increased mortality risk.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: USIDNET registry analysis (n = 1,415) confirmed that CVID-E patients exhibit significantly lower performance status, higher rates of concomitant autoimmunity (30.7%), granulomatous disease, and even malignancy. Multicenter randomized controlled trials and precision therapeutics are urgently needed to supersede the current empirical interventions with a fully evidence-based approach.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: CVID-E is pathologically determined by villous atrophy, absent mucosal plasma cells, and abundant CD8+ T cell infiltration—yielding the phenotype that often mimics celiac disease. There are three pathogenic determinants that have been elucidated so far. First, almost absent mucosal IgA is permeating and facilitating gut pathogen expansion. With this process, gut membrane lipid metabolism is shifted toward inflammatory cascades, which may render an inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)-like phenotype. Second, a mixed and specific type I/III and type II interferon release drives CD8+ T cell cytotoxicity and macrophage recruitment, producing a graft-versus-host-like mucosal damage pattern yielding apparent villous injury.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Immunoglobulin replacement does not mitigate symptoms of enteropathy, and although corticosteroids restore architecture, they impose prohibitive infectious risk. Although TNF-α blockers and thiopurines achieved complete remission in select patient cohorts, overall therapeutic response was unsatisfying. Treatment is largely empirical with limited evidence-based data.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Molecular medical tactics—employing JAK inhibitors targeting the interferon-specific pathways, namely abatacept for CTLA-4-related dysregulation—represent the most promising tool. CVID-E is a complicated disorder because it stands at the very intersection of immunodeficiency, immune dysregulation, and mucosal pathology where these determinants encompass collapsed humoral defense, gut dysbiosis, and unbalanced interferon-driven epithelial necrosis converge.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the role of norovirus in the pathogenesis of CVID-E, a noninfectious enteropathy associated with common variable immunodeficiency (CVID). CVID-E is characterized by villous atrophy, absent mucosal plasma cells, and CD8+ T cell infiltration, often mimicking celiac disease. The review highlights three pathogenic determinants: mucosal IgA deficiency leading to gut pathogen expansion, interferon-driven immune responses causing mucosal damage, and chronic norovirus infection exacerbating these pathways. Despite the potential of JAK inhibitors and abatacept, current treatments remain empirical with limited evidence-based data. The review emphasizes the need for multicenter randomized controlled trials and precision therapeutics to address the complexities of CVID-E, which involves immunodeficiency, immune dysregulation, and mucosal pathology.

title: From climate hazards to early warning: Salmonella as a sentinel for the Climate–AMR–WASH nexus

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the lack of practical biological signals linking climate hazards, WASH disruption, and emerging antimicrobial resistance (AMR) to support early prevention.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study analyzed global genomic evidence from 488,232 Salmonella genomes across 100 countries to estimate climate-associated increases in AMR-gene abundance.
analysis.methods: Whole-genome sequencing was used to distinguish clonal expansion, repeated introduction, and resistance dissemination, while culture and antimicrobial-susceptibility testing were employed for source attribution and transmission tracking.
analysis.main_results: Climate-associated increases in AMR-gene abundance were estimated in 82 of 100 countries evaluated based on global genomic evidence.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings highlight an operational gap in health systems, as they lack a practical biological signal to connect climate hazards, WASH disruption, and emerging resistance early enough for prevention.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results suggest that Salmonella can serve as a sentinel pathogen to inform WASH interventions and AMR monitoring, offering a practical tool for early warning systems.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relies on global genomic evidence and does not provide detailed statistical analyses or specific sample size information, which limits the confidence in the exact magnitude of the observed effects.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the potential of Salmonella as a sentinel pathogen for the Climate–AMR–WASH nexus, highlighting the need for a practical biological signal to connect climate hazards, water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) disruptions with emerging antimicrobial resistance (AMR). By analyzing global genomic evidence from 488,232 Salmonella genomes across 100 countries, the research estimates climate-associated increases in AMR-gene abundance. The findings suggest that Salmonella can complement existing surveillance systems and provide early warning for WASH and AMR interventions. However, the study's reliance on genomic data without detailed statistical analysis limits the confidence in its conclusions. The implications emphasize the importance of integrating climate intelligence, water safety planning, and One Health surveillance to develop effective early warning systems, while also addressing infrastructural and institutional barriers in low- and middle-income countries.

title: VIProDesign: viral protein panel design for highly variable viruses to evaluate immune responses and identify broadly neutralizing antibodies

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the challenges posed by highly mutable viruses, particularly the lack of standardized neutralization assays and up-to-date viral panels that hinder the evaluation of immunogens and identification of broadly neutralizing antibodies. This is critical for developing effective countermeasures against viruses that continuously evolve and pose major pandemic risks.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study introduced VIProDesign, a computational tool designed to generate optimized viral protein panels for rapidly evolving viruses. The tool was applied to Betacoronavirus, human immunodeficiency virus-1 (HIV-1), Influenza virus, Norovirus, and Lassa virus, with a focus on human noroviruses and their associated disease.
analysis.methods: The methods involved using the Partitioning Around Medoids (PAM) algorithm to select representative strains and applying the elbow-point method based on cumulative Shannon entropy to balance diversity and panel size. The tool was tested on various viral species, including Norovirus, to evaluate its effectiveness in generating representative panels.
analysis.main_results: VIProDesign successfully generated optimized panels for Betacoronavirus, HIV-1, Influenza virus, Norovirus, and Lassa virus. The tool supports customizable panel sizes, making it suitable for both resource-limited contexts and early-stage research. Its flexible approach streamlines viral panel design across diverse pathogens.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the results as demonstrating the utility of VIProDesign in creating representative viral panels that address sequence diversity. The novelty lies in the application of the elbow-point method based on Shannon entropy to balance panel size and diversity, which is a new approach in viral protein panel design.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the development of standardized neutralization assays and up-to-date viral panels, which are essential for evaluating immunogens and identifying broadly neutralizing antibodies. This has direct implications for improving surveillance and response strategies against rapidly evolving viruses like Norovirus.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to abstract-only evidence, which may not fully capture the practical implementation of VIProDesign. The evidence strength is moderate, as the results are based on computational methods and do not include empirical validation from real-world applications.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces VIProDesign, a computational tool for designing viral protein panels that address the high sequence diversity of rapidly evolving viruses. The tool uses the PAM algorithm and the elbow-point method based on cumulative Shannon entropy to balance diversity and panel size. It was applied to Norovirus and other viruses, demonstrating its flexibility and utility in generating representative panels for immunological and virological research. The findings suggest that VIProDesign can improve the evaluation of immunogens and the identification of broadly neutralizing antibodies, which is crucial for developing effective countermeasures. However, the study is based on abstract-only evidence, limiting the confidence in its practical implementation. The evidence is considered moderate in strength due to the lack of empirical validation from real-world applications.
